situation: I'm a senior backend engineer at a mid-size fintech in Austin, four years in. Next week I have to ask my manager for a 15% raise.

scenario.title: The 15% Ask
scenario.setting: A 30-minute 1:1 in a small conference room at a mid-size fintech office in Austin. Performance review season is approaching and budgets are tight.
scenario.user_role: You are a senior backend engineer at a mid-size fintech in Austin, four years in. You are meeting with your manager to ask for a raise.
scenario.user_goal: Ask your manager for a 15% raise next week and get a clear path to a decision.
user_knows: You have worked at this mid-size fintech in Austin for four years as a senior backend engineer
You are planning to ask for a 15% raise
You will need to make your case in the meeting using your own reasons and facts

cast.name: Ryan Parker
cast.appearance: Early 40s, polo and jeans, laptop open with a calendar full of back-to-backs
cast.voice: Friendly but rushed, practical, uses budget and process language
cast.goal: Keep you motivated and retain you without breaking his team merit budget or creating a precedent he can't defend to his boss
cast.secret: He can approve up to 5% on his own, but anything above 10% requires a VP-approved written business case submitted by end of next week
cast.reveal_when: asks directly what process or approval would be needed for an above-range increase
red_lines: Will not commit to a specific raise number in this meeting
Will not discuss other teammates' pay
cast.history: Ryan has been your direct manager for the last two years on the backend payments team. In your last 1:1 you wrapped up sprint progress and he gave you a heads-up that performance review season was coming with tight budgets.

scenario.opening_line: Hey, thanks for grabbing time — I know we just synced on sprint stuff last week and we've still got our regular 1:1 next week, so what's top of mind for today? I've got about 30 minutes.
phases: Pushback on budget and performance bar and agreeing on next steps

events.description: Ryan glances at his laptop and says he has a hard stop soon for an incident review, so you need to get to the point.
Ryan gets a Slack ping about headcount planning and reminds you this is a tough quarter for the whole org.

success_criteria: State the specific 15% ask clearly with a work-related reason
Ask about concrete next steps, timeline, or decision criteria instead of accepting a vague deferral
Stay calm and professional when challenged on budget or performance expectations
